item.title: Knee — Muscle Energy Application
clinicalUse: Use when assessment identifies a relevant impairment in Knee and the parent technique fits the patient's presentation.
Primary treatment target: knee flexion/extension, patellofemoral/tibiofemoral symptoms and functional loading.
Retain the technique only if it produces a meaningful within-session improvement.
patientPosition: Supine, prone or sitting with the knee supported in the position required by the technique.
therapistPosition: Stand beside the knee with hands close to the joint line and the limb fully supported.
stabilization: Stabilize femur, tibia or patella depending on the target.
contact: Use broad contact and avoid sustained compression over the fibular head/common peroneal nerve.
Position the target muscle/joint at a comfortable barrier and provide matched resistance without allowing unwanted movement.
forceDirection: Use a gentle isometric contraction, commonly about 10–30% effort, followed by relaxation and taking up the newly available range.
dosage: Usually 3–5 cycles of 5–10 second contractions before reassessment.
steps: 1. Record the exact comparable sign for Knee: knee flexion/extension, patellofemoral/tibiofemoral symptoms and functional loading.
2. Screen regional red flags, contraindications and technique-specific precautions before touching the patient.
3. Position and stabilize the patient so the target is comfortable and the manual input can be localized.
4. Apply a low-force trial using the parent technique principles and the region-specific contact described above.
5. Monitor pain quality, symptom distribution, guarding and patient confidence throughout.
6. Re-test the original comparable sign immediately after the trial.
7. Keep the technique only when the response is useful, then transfer the gain into active movement, loading or self-management.
mistakes: Applying the technique because it is familiar rather than because the examination supports it.
Using more force when the response is unclear or worsening.
Failing to re-test the exact movement or function that justified the treatment.
safety: Avoid routine manual therapy with suspected DVT, fracture, acute instability, infection or uncleared postoperative restriction.
Stop or modify if symptoms peripheralize, neurological status worsens, the response is disproportionate or the patient asks to stop.
item.visualCue: Knee assessment → correct regional setup → Muscle Energy Application → immediate comparable-sign re-test.

subTechniques.name: Hamstrings — MET
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Improve hamstring-related posterior-thigh restriction and straight-leg-raise tolerance when muscle length is clinically relevant.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Supine. Flex the hip with the knee near extension until the first comfortable hamstring barrier; keep the pelvis neutral and the opposite leg supported.
subTechniques.contact: One hand supports the distal leg/heel. The other stabilizes the thigh or pelvis so the patient cannot posteriorly tilt the pelvis to escape the barrier.
subTechniques.direction: Ask the patient to gently push the heel downward into hip extension against the therapist's resistance. After 5–10 seconds, relax completely and move only to the new comfortable SLR barrier.
subTechniques.dosage: 3–5 contractions at roughly 10–20% effort. No bouncing and no painful end-range stretch.
subTechniques.reassess: Straight-leg raise angle, active knee extension and a functional bend/reach task.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: A stronger contraction is not better. Low-load contraction plus a clean pelvic position usually gives a more useful response.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Stop if symptoms feel neural rather than muscular or if pain radiates distally.

subTechniques.name: Quadriceps / Rectus Femoris — MET
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Improve knee-flexion tolerance and anterior-thigh tightness when quadriceps/rectus femoris restriction is clinically relevant.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Prone or side-lying. Flex the knee to the first comfortable anterior-thigh barrier while keeping the pelvis neutral; add only a small amount of hip extension if rectus femoris is the target.
subTechniques.contact: Stabilize the pelvis/hip with one hand and control the distal tibia/ankle with the other.
subTechniques.direction: Ask the patient to gently straighten the knee against resistance. Relax fully, then increase knee flexion only to the new comfortable barrier without lumbar extension or pelvic lift.
subTechniques.dosage: 3–5 contractions of 5–10 seconds at low effort.
subTechniques.reassess: Knee flexion ROM, prone knee bend/Ely-type response and squat or stair comfort.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: Pelvic stabilization is essential. If the pelvis tips forward or the lumbar spine extends, the technique loses specificity.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Avoid forceful knee flexion after acute knee injury or when postoperative flexion limits are present.

subTechniques.name: Gastrocnemius — MET
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Improve ankle dorsiflexion with the knee extended when gastrocnemius length is a limiting factor.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Supine or long sitting with the knee straight. Move the ankle into dorsiflexion to the first comfortable calf barrier.
subTechniques.contact: Stabilize the tibia and hold the calcaneus/forefoot so the movement occurs at the ankle rather than through midfoot collapse.
subTechniques.direction: Ask the patient to gently plantarflex against resistance. Relax, then take up the new dorsiflexion range with the knee still extended.
subTechniques.reassess: Weight-bearing lunge with knee straight, ankle dorsiflexion and gait push-off/stride.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: Compare knee-straight and knee-bent dorsiflexion; that helps separate gastrocnemius from soleus limitation.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Do not apply calf manual techniques when DVT is suspected.
